reference.source: Standard gynaecology textbook and paediatric and adolescent gynaecology guidance
clinicalPearls: A transverse vaginal septum is a horizontal partition across the vaginal canal caused by faulty fusion or canalisation between the Mullerian ducts and the urogenital sinus
When the septum is complete it obstructs menstrual outflow, so adolescents typically present with primary amenorrhoea and cyclical pelvic pain despite normal secondary sexual characteristics
Retained menstrual blood accumulates above the septum causing haematocolpos and haematometra, mirroring an imperforate hymen but at a higher level in the vagina
The distinguishing feature from imperforate hymen is that the introitus and hymenal ring look normal, and the obstruction is felt higher up rather than as a bulging membrane at the opening
A perforate (incomplete) septum may allow menstruation but can cause obstructed drainage, chronic discharge, or difficulty with tampon use and intercourse
The thickness and level of the septum, which determine surgical difficulty, are best defined before treatment, usually with magnetic resonance imaging
Treatment is surgical excision of the septum with re-anastomosis of the upper and lower vaginal segments, and thick or high septa may require complex reconstruction
Because it is a Mullerian anomaly, associated renal and skeletal malformations should be sought
reference.pathophysiology: The vagina forms from fusion of the paired Mullerian (paramesonephric) ducts with the urogenital sinus, followed by canalisation of the intervening vaginal plate. A transverse septum arises when there is incomplete fusion at the junction of these components or failure of the vaginal plate to canalise fully, leaving a fibrous or fibromuscular partition at any level of the vagina. A complete septum blocks the egress of menstrual blood once cycles begin, producing haematocolpos above the obstruction and, with time, haematometra and possible retrograde menstruation. Ovarian and endocrine function are normal, so puberty progresses despite the outflow obstruction.
additionalDifferentials: Obstructed hemivagina with a longitudinal septum
Androgen insensitivity syndrome and other causes of primary amenorrhoea
additionalInvestigations: Genital examination confirming a normal introitus with obstruction higher in the vagina
Pelvic ultrasound to demonstrate haematocolpos and haematometra
Magnetic resonance imaging to define the level, thickness, and completeness of the septum and plan surgery
Assessment of pubertal development and secondary sexual characteristics
Renal tract and skeletal imaging for associated congenital anomalies
redFlags: A thick or high septum implying complex reconstructive surgery and risk of stenosis
Acute urinary retention or severe pain from a large obstructed collection
Signs of infection within retained blood
Uncertainty distinguishing septum from cervical or vaginal agenesis, which alters management
reference.prognosis: After appropriate surgical correction the outlook for menstruation and fertility is generally good, but thick or high septa carry a higher risk of postoperative stenosis and may need repeat procedures, and delayed treatment increases the chance of endometriosis from retrograde flow.
pitfalls: Mistaking a transverse septum for an imperforate hymen and planning inadequate surgery
Operating without magnetic resonance imaging to characterise septal thickness and level
Underestimating the risk of postoperative vaginal stenosis after excision of a thick septum
Attributing primary amenorrhoea with normal development to hormonal causes and missing the obstruction
Overlooking associated renal or skeletal anomalies
references: Standard gynaecology reference text on Mullerian anomalies
